title: A small HER2 reader for routine H&E slides: real-world deployment
comment: 32 pages, 12 figures, 17 tables (including supplementary material). Research use only. Weights and data: this https URL
summary: HER2 status decides who receives HER2-targeted therapy. Pathologists score HER2 protein by immunohistochemistry (IHC); equivocal IHC 2+ tumours, their hardest calls, wait for in situ hybridisation (ISH). We built a HER2 reader for routine H&E slides, owned end to end, as a baseline for pathologists. A 22M-parameter ViT-S/16 tile encoder was trained on public TCGA slides by self-supervision, distillation from H-optimus-0 and two rounds of JEPA refinement; five cross-validated attention-based slide classifiers average their probabilities; and an operating point is fixed on training data. Compared under one paired ten-seed protocol, readers on our encoder rank first of 7 on external validation from TCGA-BRCA to Yale-HER2 (AUC 0.812), level with readers on encoders 4 and 50 times larger. We also rebuilt PathBench's encoder benchmark on public cohorts; our replica reproduces its published order of reference encoders, and under it our encoder ranks first of 7 on TCGA-BRCA (0.689) and sits level with H-optimus-0 and Phikon on Yale-HER2 (0.897). On three external hospitals our deployed reader reaches AUC 0.82 on Yale-HER2 (about 0.81 with training slides balanced for tissue size), 0.75 on HEROHE and 0.63 on BCNB biopsies, and among HEROHE's 85 IHC 2+ cases it ranks ISH-amplified above non-amplified tumours at 0.76, best among our TCGA-trained readers. Per-laboratory score normalisation and a laboratory's own slides improve it further on a new site. Without a GPU our reader needs 5-6 s per slide. It serves as a research-use pre-read in a pathology platform, where it proposes a probability and a call beside IHC and helps prioritise ISH for equivocal cases. Weights, per-slide predictions and the data behind every figure are public at this https URL.

AI.tldr: The researchers developed a highly efficient, specialized Vision Transformer (ViT) model to automate HER2 status assessment from H&E slides, specifically targeting the difficult 'equivocal 2+' classification problem.
AI.motivation: HER2 status is critical for targeted therapy. Determining 'equivocal' (IHC 2+) cases is a major bottleneck in pathology, usually requiring time-consuming in situ hybridization (ISH).
AI.method: The team built a 22M-parameter ViT-S/16 tile encoder using self-supervision, distillation from H-optimus-0, and JEPA (Joint-Embedding Predictive Architecture) refinement. The system uses an ensemble of five cross-validated attention-based classifiers.
AI.result: The model achieved an AUC of 0.812 on the Yale-HER2 external dataset, outperforming or matching several much larger models. It successfully ranked ISH-amplified cases above non-amplified cases in complex IHC 2+ cohorts.
AI.conclusion: The model acts as an efficient 'pre-read' tool. It is computationally lightweight (5-6s per slide without a GPU) and helps pathologists prioritize ISH testing for equivocal cases through automated probability scoring.

title: Learning from Expert-Corrected Misdiagnoses: A Self-Evolving Consultation Agent for Traditional Chinese Medicine after Failed Treatment
summary: In traditional Chinese medicine (TCM), treatment follows syndrome differentiation (bianzheng), the step that maps a patient's findings to a TCM syndrome. A misdiagnosed syndrome therefore leads directly to inappropriate treatment, and the error usually surfaces only after that treatment fails. The physician who sees the patient next must diagnose a condition already altered by the wrong therapy, identify the initial physician's error, and avoid continuing the failed therapeutic direction. We introduce TCM-MisDx, an interactive benchmark of 820 consultations after treatment failure built from three published monographs of TCM misdiagnosis cases. An agent gathers symptoms, tongue and pulse findings through the four diagnostic methods before reporting the current syndrome, the initial error, and a corrective treatment plan. We further present TCM-SEA, a self-evolving consultation agent that rewrites its own clinical skill document: failed consultations are compared with the expert physician's documented analysis, the agent proposes a minimal edit, and the edit is kept only if it passes an acceptance gate on held-in and held-out cases. The underlying language model is never updated. On the sealed test set, TCM-SEA raises the composite score from 61.8 to 65.5, syndrome accuracy from 53.9 to 57.2 and treatment-principle accuracy from 44.7 to 48.9, and lowers the therapeutic momentum rate, the fraction of corrective plans that keep the initial physician's failed direction, from 44.1 to 38.2. Learning from expert cases outperforms learning from outcome feedback alone, with the largest gains on the monograph of inappropriate-treatment cases. The two accepted edits are short, human-readable clinical checklists that physicians can audit directly.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces a new benchmark and a self-evolving AI agent designed to identify and correct misdiagnoses in Traditional Chinese Medicine (TCM).
AI.motivation: In TCM, incorrect 'syndrome differentiation' leads to failed treatments, creating a cycle where subsequent physicians may struggle to identify the original error due to the altered state of the patient.
AI.method: 1. **TCM-MisDx**: An interactive benchmark of 820 clinical cases involving treatment failures. 2. **TCM-SEA**: A self-evolving agent that improves by comparing its performance against expert analyses. Instead of retraining the model, it iteratively updates a 'clinical skill document' (a human-readable checklist) via minimal edits that pass a validation gate.
AI.result: The TCM-SEA agent improved composite scores (61.8 to 65.5), syndrome accuracy, and treatment-principle accuracy. Crucially, it reduced the 'therapeutic momentum rate' (repeating the original error) from 44.1% to 38.2%.
AI.conclusion: Learning from expert clinical reasoning is more effective than learning from outcome feedback alone. The resulting improvements are stored in short, auditable checklists rather than black-box model weights.

title: Intervention-Conditioned Counterfactual Human Digital Twin Generator
summary: Chronic diseases evolve through long, heterogeneous trajectories shaped by interacting mediators, confounders, and treatment histories. Estimating long-term patient trajectories under alternative interventions is essential for in silico clinical trial design. However, most existing models overlook irregular visit intervals and cross-mediator dependencies, both of which are crucial for reliable long-term longitudinal prediction. Moreover, these models typically focus on outcome prediction rather than generating complete patient-state trajectories. To address these challenges, we propose CHDT, an intervention-conditioned Human Digital Twin generator under standard identification assumptions for multimodal longitudinal trajectory estimation. Its main empirical advantage arises from explicit modeling of irregular visit intervals, while cross-mediator refinement provides additional gains in selected intervention-conditioned settings. Across real-world ADNI and simulator-generated ALPACA cohorts, CHDT shows improved long-horizon patient-state fidelity relative to competing baselines. Ablation results indicate that irregular-time conditioning provides the primary empirical gain, and cross-mediator refinement provides additional improvements.

AI.tldr: CHDT is a new framework for generating long-term patient-state trajectories under different interventions, specifically addressing irregular visit intervals and cross-mediator dependencies in multimodal longitudinal data.
AI.motivation: Current models for chronic disease trajectory estimation often fail to account for irregular visit intervals, cross-mediator dependencies, and the need for generating complete patient-state trajectories rather than just outcome prediction.
AI.method: The proposed CHDT (intervention-conditioned Human Digital Twin) uses explicit modeling of irregular visit intervals and cross-mediator refinement under standard identification assumptions to estimate multimodal longitudinal trajectories.
AI.result: CHDT demonstrated superior long-horizon patient-state fidelity compared to baselines in ADNI and ALPACA datasets, with irregular-time conditioning identified as the primary driver of performance gain.
AI.conclusion: CHDT effectively handles the complexities of longitudinal patient data, providing a more reliable tool for in silico clinical trial design through improved trajectory generation.

title: Recycle only when you have to!
summary: AlphaFold 3-like models (e.g., Boltz, Protenix, etc.) have pushed the frontier of protein binder design. This architecture is used both for the generation of binder candidates (e.g., by hallucination or converting these models into backbone or full atom generative models) as well as for the screening of these candidates for valid binders. In this paper, we start from the observation that AlphaFold 3's confidence metrics (ipSAE, ipTM) as well as structural consistency metrics can be predicted directly from the trunk even at early recycling. Because our proposed predictor is cheap, differentiable, and available at every cycle, it can be used in two distinct ways: as a decision signal to wisely spend the recycling budget for screening and as an objective for hallucination-based design. We show that both applications lead to increased performance at significantly reduced computational cost.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces a lightweight, differentiable predictor that estimates AlphaFold 3-style confidence metrics (ipSAE, ipTM) and structural consistency early in the model's recycling process.
AI.motivation: Current protein binder design via AlphaFold 3-like models is computationally expensive, especially when performing high-throughput screening or hallucination-based generation.
AI.method: The authors developed a 'cheap' predictor that can extract confidence signals directly from the model's trunk during the early recycling stages, rather than waiting for the final output.
AI.result: The predictor is applied in two ways: (1) as an early-exit signal to save computation during screening, and (2) as a differentiable loss function to guide binder design (hallucination). Both methods improve performance while significantly reducing computational overhead.
AI.conclusion: Predicting structural quality mid-process enables more efficient and effective generative design of protein binders.

title: Physics-Grounded Simulation Enables Zero-Shot Molecular and Reaction Analysis in Scanning Tunneling Microscopy
summary: Quantitative identification of molecular products and reaction pathways from scanning tunneling microscopy images is difficult when labeled images are unavailable for a new chemical system. We develop a simulation-assisted framework for zero-shot analysis that requires only precursor information for a new target system, with no experimental images or annotations from that system used during model training. The framework couples two functional components: NanoSim generates physics-grounded synthetic images from predicted reaction products and sampled surface scenes, while NanoAnalysis translates molecular detections into product populations, spatial arrangements, and mechanistic interpretations. Applied to a representative on-surface reaction, the detector achieves a micro-averaged F1 score of 0.92 on experimental images. Analysis of the detected molecules reveals annealing-dependent population changes and reaction-site preferences consistent with experimental observations. Beyond this capability, its modular organization allows heterogeneous data from other systems to be used to improve each component independently, providing a scalable route for continued generalization.

AI.tldr: A zero-shot framework using simulation-based synthetic data to identify molecular products and reaction pathways in STM images without requiring labeled experimental data.
AI.motivation: The difficulty of quantitative identification of molecular products and reaction pathways in STM when labeled images for new chemical systems are unavailable.
AI.method: A simulation-assisted framework coupling NanoSim (generates physics-grounded synthetic images from precursor/product info) and NanoAnalysis (translates molecular detections into spatial and mechanistic data).
AI.result: Achieved a micro-averaged F1 score of 0.92 on experimental images and successfully identified annealing-dependent population changes and reaction-site preferences.
AI.conclusion: The framework provides a scalable, zero-shot approach for molecular analysis in STM imaging, capable of accurately interpreting reaction pathways and molecular populations through a modular, simulation-assisted design.

title: Tree-based Algorithms for Breakpoint Median and Near-Median Genomes
summary: Median genomes serve as candidates for ancestral reconstruction and help study the diversity of parsimonious rearrangement solutions. However, the breakpoint median problem is NP-hard for unichromosomal genomes, and medians are non-unique, making their diversity important to study. In this paper, we develop tree-based algorithms for studying breakpoint medians of linear unichromosomal genomes represented as unsigned permutations. The algorithms construct rooted labeled trees whose leaves encode candidate median genomes satisfying local adjacency constraints derived from the inputs. We show that the resulting reduced search spaces contain all breakpoint medians while being much smaller than the full permutation space. We investigate these reduced spaces experimentally for three-genome instances. Our method finds exact medians and many near-optimal approximations, while early sampling of leaves often produces near-medians quickly. We also introduce constrained sampling procedures for targeting balanced near-medians, whose distances to the input genomes are more evenly distributed and hence are particularly relevant for ancestral reconstruction. The resulting framework provides a unified method for exact enumeration, efficient sampling, and targeted exploration of median and near-median genomes. In contrast to Traveling Salesman Problem-based approaches, which typically return a single solution and do not reveal the diversity or balance of the median set, our method can enumerate all medians, sample near-medians early, and target structurally distinct candidates under the breakpoint distance.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces a tree-based framework to study the diversity and distribution of median genomes for unichromosomal genomes (unsigned permutations), moving beyond finding a single solution to exploring the entire space of medians and near-medians.
AI.motivation: Finding a median genome (the genome that minimizes the sum of distances to input genomes) is NP-hard and results in non-unique solutions. Existing methods (like TSP-based approaches) typically provide only one solution and fail to capture the structural diversity of the median set.
AI.method:
The authors develop tree-based algorithms that: 
1. Construct rooted labeled trees where leaves represent candidate median genomes constrained by local adjacencies.
2. Create a significantly reduced search space that contains all possible medians.
3. Implement constrained sampling to find 'balanced' near-medians (those with evenly distributed distances to input genomes), which are crucial for ancestral reconstruction.
AI.result: The framework allows for exact enumeration of all medians, efficient sampling of near-medians, and targeted exploration of structurally distinct candidates, outperforming traditional TSP-based single-solution methods.
AI.conclusion: The method provides a unified approach for studying the diversity of ancestral reconstruction candidates, offering a more holistic view of the genomic median space than previous approaches.

title: VitisGP: Multi-Task Benchmark for Genotype to Phenotype Grapevine Prediction
summary: As climate change reshapes grape-growing conditions, predicting grapevine phenotypes from genomic variation is increasingly important for identifying and breeding cultivars suited to emerging environmental pressures. Existing research on the grapevine genotype-phenotype relationship using machine learning has often focused on individual traits, isolated regions, or a limited set of predictive models. We introduce VitisGP, a multi-phenotype curated dataset, integrating genome-wide SNP data with 26 heterogeneous phenotype prediction tasks spanning sommelier-curated aroma traits (N=11), botanical traits (N=14) and wine color---across 1,197 Vitis vinifera cultivars. We employ VitisGP to benchmark phenotype prediction, comparing machine-learning models with differing inductive biases---L2-regularized logistic regression, Random Forest, XGBoost, CatBoost, GBLUP and Transformer-based models, providing the first systematic comparison of this breadth on harmonized grapevine data. Across the benchmark, CatBoost achieves the strongest overall performance (macro-average AUROC=0.696 across 26 tasks), although model performance varies substantially across phenotype classes, with sensory and color traits showing stronger predictability than agronomic characteristics. VitisGP provides the community with a resource for investigating the genomic basis of phenotypic traits and screening grapevine diversity for climate-relevant characteristics.

AI.tldr: Introduction of VitisGP, a comprehensive multi-phenotype dataset for grapevine, used to benchmark various machine learning models for predicting diverse traits from genomic data.
AI.motivation: To address the need for predicting grapevine phenotypes from genomic variation to identify cultivars suited to climate change, moving beyond research focused on single traits or isolated regions.
AI.method: Integration of genome-wide SNP data with 26 heterogeneous phenotype prediction tasks (aroma, botanical, and color) across 1,197 cultivars, followed by benchmarking various machine learning models (Logistic Regression, Random Forest, XGBoost, CatBoost, GBLUP, and Transformers).
AI.result: CatBoost achieved the best overall performance (macro-average AUROC=0.696), with sensory and color traits showing higher predictability than agronomic traits.
AI.conclusion: VitisGP serves as a significant community resource for investigating the genomic basis of grapevine traits and screening for climate-relevant characteristics.

title: Expression of White and Gray Matter Autism Functional Network Connectivity Signatures in Infancy
comment: 5 pages, 1 figure. Submitted to the 2027 IEEE 24th International Symposium on Biomedical Imaging (ISBI)
summary: Functional connectivity studies have provided valuable insights into altered brain organization in autism spectrum disorder (ASD). However, most functional connectivity studies focus exclusively on either gray matter (GM) regions or white matter (WM) tracts and examine specific age groups, rather than investigating their functional interactions across brain development. This limits our understanding of how GM-WM functional interactions evolve developmentally and may obscure important aspects of brain network organization in ASD. We combined integrated WM+GM functional network connectivity (FNC) with brain-wide risk scores (BRSs) to quantify ASD-associated pattern expression in ABIDE I/II and an independent infant cohort. We employed a NeuroMark framework with predefined WM and GM intrinsic connectivity networks templates, to estimate subject-level FNC. First, we identified two distinct patterns of altered WM+GM FNC in ASD: GM-related hypoconnectivity centered on the paralimbic network and WM-GM hyperconnectivity centered on the frontal network. These findings highlight the involvement of higher-order cognitive networks and the importance of WM-GM functional interactions in characterizing ASD-related connectivity alterations. Second, infants with a higher familial likelihood of autism exhibited greater mean expression of ASD-associated FNC patterns than those with a lower familial likelihood, as quantified by BRS. These group-level findings do not establish developmental persistence or predict diagnostic outcomes at the individual level.

AI.tldr: The study integrates WM and GM functional connectivity to identify specific ASD-associated patterns (paralimbic hypoconnectivity and frontal hyperconnectivity) and shows these patterns are more evident in infants with higher familial risk.
AI.motivation: Existing studies often focus exclusively on either gray matter or white matter or specific age groups, limiting the understanding of how GM-WM functional interactions evolve across development in ASD.
AI.method: The researchers combined integrated WM+GM functional network connectivity (FNC) with brain-wide risk scores (BRSs) using the NeuroMark framework with predefined WM and GM intrinsic connectivity networks templates, analyzing data from ABIDE I/II and an independent infant cohort.
AI.result: Two patterns were identified: GM-related hypoconnectivity in the paralimbic network and WM-GM hyperconnectivity in the frontal network. Additionally, infants with higher familial risk scores showed greater expression of these ASD-associated FNC patterns.
AI.conclusion: The study identifies two distinct ASD-associated patterns of altered WM+GM functional network connectivity (FNC) and demonstrates that these patterns are more pronounced in infants with higher familial risk, though developmental persistence and individual-level prediction remain unproven.

title: GraphTFactor: A graph-based approach for proteins transcription factor prediction
summary: Transcription factors (TFs) play an important role in regulating gene expression, making their identification a fundamental task in computational biology. In this work, we propose GraphTFactor, a novel end-to-end framework that models protein sequences as graphs and directly classifies transcription factors. By encoding sequences into graph structures, the proposed approach naturally handles variable-length inputs while preserving relevant relational information, without imposing length constraints. Experimental results show that GraphTFactor outperforms state-of-the-art methods on benchmark datasets, demonstrating the effectiveness of graph-based representations for TF prediction while providing interpretable insights into the sequence regions contributing to the model's predictions. To support reproducibility and practical adoption, we release an open-source software package and an interactive web application that let users easily perform TF prediction on custom sequences.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces **GraphTFactor**, a new end-to-end framework that uses graph-based modeling of protein sequences to identify transcription factors (TFs) more accurately and interpretably than existing methods.
AI.motivation: Traditional methods for TF identification often struggle with variable-length protein sequences and capturing complex relational information within a sequence.
AI.method: Instead of standard linear encoding, the model represents protein sequences as **graphs**. This approach allows the framework to handle variable-length inputs naturally and preserve essential relational features between amino acids.
AI.result: GraphTFactor outperformed current state-of-the-art (SOTA) models on benchmark datasets. The model also provides **interpretability**, identifying specific sequence regions that drive the prediction.
AI.conclusion: The authors have improved TF prediction accuracy and accessibility by releasing an open-source package and an interactive web application.

title: Basis statistics for phylogenetic tree shape: tree balance formulas beyond expectations
summary: Summary statistics that measure the shapes of phylogenetic trees contributed to quantitatively understanding evolutionary processes. Among phylogenetic summary statistics, the tree balance indices have been designed to capture intuitive notions of balance or imbalance in trees. Here, we characterize the tree balance indices in terms of basis statistics, mapping the exponentially large space of rooted, binary, unlabeled trees to lower-dimensional spaces. We observe that many tree balance indices can be represented in terms of linear functions of these low-dimensional spaces, enabling us to compute exact formulas for the means, variances, and covariances of many balance indices under the Yule--Harding model. The new framework recapitulates existing formulas for the expectations of 8 indices: Sackin index, average leaf depth, total cophenetic index, $\hat{s}$-shape statistic, Colless index, corrected Colless index, quadratic Colless index, and rooted quartet index for binary trees. It produces new formulas for the expectations of 9 additional indices: equal weights Colless index, total $I$ index, total $I'$ index, Rogers $J$ index, total internal path length, total path length, average vertex depth, stairs1 index, and stairs2 index. Moreover, the framework also allows us to calculate the exact variance of all 17 indices that are represented by the bases as well as the covariance and correlation for all $\binom{17}{2} = 136$ pairs among the 17 indices.

AI.tldr: A new mathematical framework characterizes tree balance indices as linear functions of low-dimensional basis statistics, allowing for the exact calculation of means, variances, and covariances under the Yule-Harding model.
AI.motivation: To quantitatively understand evolutionary processes, researchers use summary statistics (tree balance indices) to measure tree shapes, but calculating exact distributions for these indices is computationally difficult.
AI.method: The authors map the exponentially large space of rooted, binary, unlabeled trees to lower-dimensional spaces using basis statistics, representing many balance indices as linear functions within these spaces.
AI.result: The framework successfully recapitulates existing formulas for 8 indices and provides new exact formulas for 9 additional indices, as well as exact variances and covariances for a wide range of indices.
AI.conclusion: The study provides a unified framework to characterize tree balance indices through basis statistics, enabling the calculation of exact formulas for means, variances, and covariances under the Yule-Harding model.

title: Temporal and spatial couplings in the dynamics of human walking and running
summary: Rhythmic behaviours such as walking and running are commonly modelled as dynamical systems around a stable limit cycle. To keep such models tractable, it is usually assumed that each step depends only on the previous one, that the limit cycle is fixed, and that the sagittal and frontal planes can be studied separately. Here, we test these assumptions in seven public datasets of human gait (71 participants), including 16 people who both walked and ran. We fit linear step-to-step maps and validate them by cross-validation, holding out more data where more data exist. At first sight, gait has memory: the state two steps back lowers the prediction error by up to 29\%. Yet most of this temporal coupling vanishes once the operating point may drift slowly and measurement noise is modelled; gait remains limit-cycle-like, around an operating point that moves. Running keeps more memory than walking in the same people. Spatial coupling between the planes is present in most participants, mainly from sagittal to frontal, but weak. This supports planar models of healthy gait, while a repeatable, task-dependent coupling index may serve as a measure of gait quality. The simple models are wrong, but useful enough.

AI.tldr: The study evaluates the validity of common gait modeling assumptions, finding that while gait exhibits temporal and spatial coupling, simple planar and first-order limit-cycle models remain useful for describing healthy human movement.
AI.motivation: To test common simplifying assumptions in gait modeling: that each step depends only on the previous one (Markovian), that the limit cycle is fixed, and that sagittal and frontal planes can be studied independently.
AI.method: Fitting linear step-to-step maps to seven public datasets (71 participants) and validating them using cross-validation, accounting for drifting operating points and measurement noise.
AI.result: Gait shows temporal memory (the state two steps back reduces error by up to 29%), which mostly vanishes when accounting for noise and drift; running retains more memory than walking; and weak spatial coupling exists primarily from sagittal to frontal planes.
AI.conclusion: Current simple gait models are technically inaccurate due to temporal and spatial coupling, but they are sufficiently useful for practical applications, and coupling indices could serve as measures of gait quality.

title: Contribution of chromosome-naïve transposon-seeded network of DNA templates to intracellular pools of protein dimers of liquid-liquid phase-separated condensate-forming proteins
summary: Molecular mechanisms governing protein-protein interactions (PPI) contributing to the biogenesis of membraneless condensates remain poorly understood. Observations reported in this contribution demonstrate that liquid-liquid phase-separated (LLPS) condensate-forming proteins and their variants harboring condensate-disrupting human pathogenic mutations are significantly enriched among PPI cascade constituents of the Hybrid Assembly Pathway (HAP) of endogenous multiprotein complexes (EMC). In contrast, no structured or disordered proteins defined as condensate-negative molecules were detected among PPI cascade constituents. Cumulative evidence derived from different lines of analytical inquiries support the concept of the significant contributions of PPI cascade constituents of HAP to the biogenesis of intracellular pools of cell type-specific protein heterodimers assembled with the engagement of at least one protein monomer selected from condensate-forming protein molecules. Analytical evidence documented in this study support the concept that genome-wide chromosome-naïve networks of transposon-seeded DNA-templates nucleate the initiation of PPI cascade chain reactions with the capacity to facilitate the concurrent iterative assembly in human cells of both the membraneless biomolecular condensates and the structured multiprotein complexes. AlphaFold 3D modelling of mutation patterns and analysis of partner-bound experimental structures identified variants located at a measured protein dimerization interface. This contribution nominates numerous protein heterodimers of potential relevance to human pathophysiology for follow-up mechanistic studies of potential fundamental and translational impacts.

AI.tldr: The study identifies a link between liquid-liquid phase separation (LLPS) proteins and the Hybrid Assembly Pathway (HAP), suggesting that transposon-seeded DNA templates nucleate protein-protein interaction (PPI) cascades that drive the simultaneous assembly of membraneless condensates and structured multiprotein complexes.
AI.motivation: To understand the molecular mechanisms governing protein-protein interactions (PPI) that contribute to the biogenesis of membraneless condensates, which currently remain poorly understood.
AI.method: Comparative analysis of PPI cascade constituents in the Hybrid Assembly Pathway (HAP), differential enrichment analysis between condensate-forming and condensate-negative proteins, and AlphaFold 3D modeling of mutation patterns and protein dimerization interfaces.
AI.result: Condensate-forming proteins and their pathogenic variants are significantly enriched in HAP PPI cascades, whereas condensate-negative proteins are not; additionally, mutation patterns were identified at specific protein dimerization interfaces.
AI.conclusion: Genome-wide transposon-seeded DNA templates nucleate PPI cascades that facilitate the concurrent assembly of both membraneless condensates and structured multiprotein complexes, identifying numerous heterodimers relevant to human pathophysiology.

title: D2ML: Models for Direct-to-Biology Small Molecule Screening
comment: NeurIPS 2026 Workshop on AI for Drug Discovery (AI4DD)
summary: Direct-to-biology (D2B) screening enables rapid testing of newly synthesized molecules without purification. However, uncertain concentrations in crude mixtures and limited purified-compound measurements complicate the use of these data in machine learning. Here we show that models tailored to the structure of D2B data can improve prediction and guide the discovery of more potent and selective compounds. Our assay-aware models predict activity from single-point screens, relative potency across targets from crude dose-response assays, and absolute potency from purified-compound measurements. For crude assays, potency ratios between targets tested from the same well can retain selectivity information despite uncertain concentrations. A joint model that shares information across stages and balances their contributions to training improved predictions over separate neural networks. The largest gain was in crude dose-response selectivity prediction, where rank correlation increased from 0.27 to 0.40. In a separate experiment, independently trained models guided the selection of 84 new compounds to improve ROS1 potency while limiting activity against the anti-target TRKB. Synthesis and testing identified compounds that extended the measured Pareto front, achieving better combinations of potency and selectivity than those in the training data. The most selective new compound achieved a ROS1 IC50 of 14.7 nM and 233-fold selectivity over TRKB. By comparison, the most selective training compound had a ROS1 IC50 of 20.3 nM and 79-fold selectivity. ATLAS provides the experimental setting for this approach, supporting synthesis and screening of 1,000-10,000 model-selected compounds in two- to three-week cycles. Together, these results show how assay-aware learning can use the full D2B assay sequence to guide multi-objective molecular optimization.

AI.tldr: The study introduces assay-aware machine learning models that leverage uncertain D2B screening data to successfully guide the optimization of highly potent and selective molecular compounds.
AI.motivation: Direct-to-biology (D2B) screening is fast but introduces challenges for machine learning due to uncertain concentrations in crude mixtures and limited availability of purified-compound measurements.
AI.method: The authors developed assay-aware neural networks capable of processing single-point screens, relative potency from crude dose-response assays, and absolute potency from purified compounds, using a joint model to share information across these stages.
AI.result: The models improved rank correlation for crude dose-response selectivity from 0.27 to 0.40 and successfully guided the synthesis of new compounds that outperformed the training data in potency and selectivity (e.g., 233-fold selectivity for ROS1 over TRKB).
AI.conclusion: Assay-aware learning models can effectively utilize imperfect Direct-to-biology (D2B) data to guide multi-objective molecular optimization, significantly improving the discovery of potent and selective compounds.

title: Transmission and filtering of stochastic rhythms in bursty gene expression
summary: How stochastic rhythms in upstream regulatory signals are transmitted to downstream gene expression is a fundamental question in systems biology. Although experiments have shown that molecular degradation strongly influences downstream rhythmic responses, a general quantitative theory explaining how degradation, stochastic bursting, and upstream timing variability jointly govern rhythm transmission remains lacking. Here we develop a general analytical framework based on a martingale-based orthogonal decomposition, applicable to arbitrarily complex upstream dynamics, including memory effects. We derive exact autocorrelation and power-spectrum transmission laws, establish an oscillation-efficiency contraction principle, and identify a critical degradation rate that provides a necessary and sufficient condition for stochastic rhythm transmission. An explicit rhythm-transmission relation reveals that increasing burst frequency and modulation depth promotes rhythm transmission, whereas greater variability in upstream cycle duration suppresses it. In particular, increasing burst size leaves oscillation efficiency unchanged. The predicted degradation threshold correctly separates all ten pulsing and nonpulsing p53 target proteins reported in previous experiments. These results provide a theoretical foundation for understanding how cells selectively preserve or integrate rhythmic regulatory signals.

AI.tldr: The paper presents a new theoretical framework to understand how cells transmit rhythmic signals from upstream regulators to downstream genes, accounting for noise and degradation.
AI.motivation: Existing models could not quantitatively explain how the interplay between molecular degradation, stochastic bursting, and upstream timing variability affects the transmission of rhythmic signals.
AI.method: The authors developed an analytical framework using 'martingale-based orthogonal decomposition.' This approach allows for the modeling of complex upstream dynamics, including memory effects, to derive exact laws for autocorrelation and power-spectrum transmission.
AI.result:
1. **Oscillation-Efficiency Contraction Principle**: Established how rhythmicity is lost during transmission.
2. **Critical Degradation Rate**: Identified a mathematical threshold that determines whether a rhythm is transmitted or lost.
3. **Parameter Effects**: Found that higher burst frequency and modulation depth improve transmission, while upstream timing variability suppresses it. Interestingly, burst size does not affect oscillation efficiency.
4. **Biological Validation**: The model successfully predicted the rhythmic behavior (pulsing vs. non-pulsing) of ten different p53 target proteins.
AI.conclusion: The study provides a general quantitative theory to explain how cells selectively filter or preserve rhythmic regulatory signals amidst stochastic noise.

title: Co$^2$ODE: Conditionally Coarse-Grained Model Discovery for Rewiring in Biochemical Networks
summary: Biochemical networks propagate the signals that regulate cellular behaviour, and which routes carry them depends on cellular context: a shift in context rewires the network's effective dynamics. Mechanistic simulators are misspecified here because the effective dynamics emerge from an interaction structure that is only partially known. Model discovery instead learns the dynamics from data, but sparse, correlated measurements poorly identify a full network model. What matters is narrower: the portion the context rewires. We introduce conditionally coarse-grained ODEs (Co$^2$ODE), which model that portion as a sparse neural or symbolic ODE: a conditional mask selects the markers carrying the rewiring, and a variational autoencoder compresses the remaining markers into a learnt closure term. On single-cell phosphoproteomic data spanning 30 cancer-relevant overexpressions, Co$^2$ODE compresses a 30-marker panel into a 10-dimensional state while matching the predictive accuracy of a neural ODE fit to the full panel. The closure absorbs what the mask drops, hence the accuracy is insensitive to which markers are kept. Adding a prior score to the loss shifts the selected markers at no cost in fit, indicating the data are not interventional enough to identify the underlying biology.

AI.tldr: Co2ODE models context-dependent biochemical network rewiring by using a conditional mask for key markers and a VAE for a closure term, achieving high accuracy through dimensionality reduction.
AI.motivation: Biochemical networks change dynamics based on cellular context, but existing mechanistic simulators are misspecified due to incomplete interaction knowledge, and standard model discovery fails due to sparse, correlated measurements.
AI.method: Introduced Co2ODE (conditionally coarse-grained ODEs), which uses a conditional mask to select rewiring markers for a sparse neural/symbolic ODE and a variational autoencoder to compress the remaining markers into a learned closure term.
AI.result: Applied to single-cell phosphoproteomic data, Co2ODE compressed a 30-marker panel into a 10-dimensional state while maintaining the predictive accuracy of a full-panel neural ODE.
AI.conclusion: Co2ODE successfully models context-dependent rewiring in biochemical networks by separating markers into a sparse dynamic component and a compressed closure term, though lack of interventional data limits the ability to recover the exact biological structure.

title: Hyperbolic embedding of higher-order simplicial networks
summary: Many biological interactions involve groups rather than pairs, as when several proteins assemble into a multi-protein complex. Simplicial complexes naturally capture these collective interactions. Existing hyperbolic embeddings represent network hierarchy and similarity through a few interpretable coordinates, but rely only on pairwise links: they cannot distinguish three units engaged in a common interaction from three units connected only in pairs. We introduce here the hyperbolic higher-order (HHO) embedding, which embeds a simplicial complex into the Poincaré disk, while incorporating its group interactions. The hyperbolic area of the triangle spanned by three interacting nodes then measures how compactly their interaction is represented. Testson synthetic and real-world networks, including a co-authorship network and the protein interaction network of \textit{Escherichia coli}, show that HHO reduces the hyperbolic area of triangles representing simplices relative to those obtained from pairwise network embeddings. HHO also recovers node groups more accurately than pairwise embeddings and a weighted-clique alternative, with performance competitive with Euclidean embeddings, while providing a low-dimensional representation that can be analyzed with the tools of network geometry.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces Hyperbolic Higher-Order (HHO) embedding, a method to represent simplicial complexes (group interactions) in hyperbolic space, outperforming traditional pairwise embeddings in capturing multi-node relationships.
AI.motivation: Existing hyperbolic embeddings are limited to pairwise links. They fail to distinguish between a group of three units interacting collectively (a simplex) versus three units connected only by individual pairs.
AI.method: HHO embeds simplicial complexes into the Poincaré disk. It uses the hyperbolic area of triangles spanned by interacting nodes as a metric to measure the compactness and strength of group interactions.
AI.result: HHO successfully reduces the hyperbolic area of triangles for simplices compared to pairwise models. It outperforms pairwise and weighted-clique embeddings in recovering node groups and remains competitive with Euclidean embeddings while maintaining low-dimensional geometric interpretability.
AI.conclusion: HHO provides a scalable, low-dimensional, and geometrically interpretable way to model higher-order biological and social interactions.

title: An extension of the classic Buneman theorem from phylogenetic trees to networks
summary: Phylogenetic networks provide a natural framework for representing reticulate evolutionary events such as horizontal gene transfer and hybridization. In the present manuscript, we investigate the identifiability of phylogenetic networks under (hardwired) parsimony, a natural extension of Maximum Parsimony from trees to networks. More precisely, we ask which structural features of a network can be uniquely inferred from so-called $A_k$-alignments under this criterion. While identifiability has been studied extensively for phylogenetic trees under parsimony, little is known about the identifiability of networks under hardwired parsimony. We take a first step towards addressing this gap by developing a general framework for studying identifiability under hardwired parsimony. We then use this framework to show that the tree of blobs of a phylogenetic network can be reconstructed from its $A_1$-alignment. This result can be viewed as a natural extension of Buneman's well-known splits equivalence theorem. Finally, we show that, under hardwired parsimony, cycles of length at least $5$ cannot in general be uniquely identified from character data, establishing a fundamental limitation of hardwired parsimony.

AI.tldr: The paper investigates the identifiability of phylogenetic networks using the 'hardwired parsimony' criterion, establishing a framework to determine which network features can be uniquely reconstructed from character data.
AI.motivation: While identifiability under parsimony is well-studied for phylogenetic trees, there is a significant research gap regarding the identifiability of reticulate evolutionary structures (networks) under the hardwired parsimony extension.
AI.method: The authors develop a general mathematical framework for studying identifiability under hardwired parsimony and analyze the reconstructability of network components using $A_k$-alignments.
AI.result: The study proves that the 'tree of blobs' in a phylogenetic network can be reconstructed from its $A_1$-alignment (extending Buneman's theorem) but also demonstrates that cycles of length 5 or greater cannot be uniquely identified.
AI.conclusion: Hardwired parsimony allows for the reconstruction of certain macro-structures like the tree of blobs, but it faces fundamental limitations in identifying larger cycles within a network.

title: Automatic Construction of Strong Simple Baselines
summary: To rigorously establish the value of a novel deep learning method, it must be compared against appropriate baselines. As deep learning has become increasingly common in the physical and life sciences, there have been numerous cases in which apparent progress has turned out to be an artifact of omitted or missing baselines. In this work, we investigate whether this problem can be mitigated by using large language models to automate the construction of baselines. We assemble 36 supervised classification and regression tasks from peer-reviewed studies in Nature, Science, and Cell-family journals that investigate novel deep learning methods for scientific applications. We then use a language model to construct simple baselines for each task. These automatically constructed baselines are strong, recovering a median of 95.5% (mean 85.7%) of the gap between a trivial predictor and the score of the deep learning model. The median simple baseline matches or exceeds the performance of the deep learning model in 12 studies. We further examine the variation across scientific domains and publication venues and we characterize the effects of test-time compute and access to different levels of study context. As human peer review has struggled to keep up with the rapidly increasing volume of research articles in recent years, our results suggest that automated baseline construction is a practical and scalable check on deep learning contributions in the physical and life sciences.

AI.tldr: This paper proposes using LLMs to automatically generate strong baselines for scientific deep learning tasks to detect cases where reported progress is merely an artifact of missing comparisons.
AI.motivation: Deep learning progress in physical and life sciences is often overstated because studies frequently omit or miss appropriate baselines, making it difficult for human peer reviewers to keep up with the volume of research.
AI.method: The researchers assembled 36 supervised classification and regression tasks from high-impact scientific journals and used a language model to automatically construct simple baseline models for each task.
AI.result: The LLM-constructed baselines are strong, recovering a median of 95.5% of the gap between a trivial predictor and the DL model; they matched or exceeded DL model performance in 12 out of 36 studies.
AI.conclusion: Automated baseline construction using LLMs is a practical and scalable way to validate deep learning contributions in scientific research, mitigating the issue of missing baselines in peer review.

title: Immersed Boundary Electrodiffusion in the Wasserstein Gradient Flow Formalism: Global Well-Posedness, Non-Equilibrium Thermodynamics, and Singular Asymptotics
summary: We introduce a unified optimal transport framework for the Immersed Boundary (IB) electrodiffusion active pump model. By representing membrane chemical potential barriers and active pump potentials via smoothed Eulerian kernels ($\Psi_w, \mathcal{H}_w$), we formulate the passive dynamics as an $L^2$-Wasserstein ($W_2$) gradient flow coupled to non-conservative active pushing fields representing ATP-driven $3:2$ $\text{Na}^+/\text{K}^+$ exchangers. We establish global weak existence of solutions to the continuous Poisson--Nernst--Planck--IB system via a split-step Jordan--Kinderlehrer--Otto (JKO) variational scheme, backed by Calderón--Zygmund bounds for non-local Poisson drift and $H^3(\mathbb{S}^1)$ interface regularity under Stokes flow. We prove the continuous Rayleighian energy balance and establish exponential $W_2$-stability of Non-Equilibrium Steady States (NESS) under a quantitative Bakry--Émery curvature threshold. Furthermore, we analyze the dual singular limits of kernel smoothing width $w \to 0$ and dimensionless Debye length $g = \lambda_D / L \to 0$. We establish the precise asymptotic regime connecting regularized and sharp models, prove the $\Gamma$-convergence of regularized energy functionals, derive distributional interface flux jump conditions, and resolve $O(\lambda_D)$ Debye space-charge boundary layers to confirm bulk electroneutrality.

AI.tldr: The paper presents a rigorous mathematical framework for modeling biological electrodiffusion using an Immersed Boundary (IB) approach, integrated with Optimal Transport theory.
AI.motivation: To model the complex dynamics of active ion pumps (like Na+/K+ exchangers) within an electrodiffusion system while maintaining mathematical rigor and stability.
AI.method: 1. **Framework**: Uses a $W_2$ (Wasserstein-2) gradient flow for passive dynamics, coupled with non-conservative fields for active pumping. 2. **Numerical/Existence Scheme**: Implements a split-step JKO (Jordan–Kinderlehrer–Otto) variational scheme. 3. **Mathematical Tools**: Employs Calderón–Zygmund bounds for Poisson drift and $\Gamma$-convergence for singular limits.
AI.result: 1. **Existence**: Proved global weak existence of solutions for the Poisson–Nernst–Planck–IB system. 2. **Stability**: Established exponential $W_2$-stability of Non-Equilibrium Steady States (NESS). 3. **Asymptotics**: Successfully resolved the limits of kernel smoothing ($w \to 0$) and Debye length ($g \to 0$), deriving jump conditions and confirming bulk electroneutrality.
AI.conclusion: The study provides a consistent bridge between regularized (smooth) models and sharp interface models, ensuring that the mathematical approximations remain physically valid in the limit of vanishing thickness and smoothing.

title: Localizing predictive concepts encoded in neural representations via hierarchical testing
summary: Understanding which regulatory sequence motifs a genomic deep learning model has learned, with statistical error guarantees, is essential for trusting its use in downstream tasks such as variant effect prediction. Existing approaches to identifying which units in a trained network encode human- understandable concepts fall into two groups. Exploratory methods rank and visualize units but offer no statistical guarantee that the selected units are associated with the prediction target across the population of inputs. Testing-based methods test only single units or one pre-defined set of them, and do not control the error across the many sets of units. We introduce CUTTIE (Cluster-tree Unit Top-down Testing of Independence with Error control), which clusters the units of each layer into a tree and tests the clusters top-down with conditional independence tests, localizing information about the target while controlling the family-wise error rate. Thereby, we identify clusters that carry information about the target beyond the rest of the layer. For the units in the identified clusters, conditional attribution maps then reveal what motifs they encode. In a controlled simulation, the procedure identifies the clusters whose concepts affect the target. We apply the procedure to a convolutional model predicting cell-type-specific chromatin accessibility from DNA sequence, where the concepts encoded in the identified clusters map onto known regulatory motifs.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces **CUTTIE**, a new statistical framework designed to identify which specific units (neurons/filters) in genomic deep learning models represent human-understandable regulatory motifs, while providing rigorous error guarantees.
AI.motivation: Current methods for interpreting genomic models are either purely exploratory (lacking statistical rigor) or testing-based (failing to control error when testing multiple groups of units simultaneously).
AI.method: CUTTIE uses a **top-down clustering approach**: 1) It organizes units of a layer into a tree structure. 2) It performs conditional independence tests on these clusters. 3) It controls the **Family-Wise Error Rate (FWER)** to ensure findings are statistically significant. 4) It uses conditional attribution maps to decode the specific motifs within identified clusters.
AI.result: 1) **Simulation:** Successfully identifies clusters linked to target concepts. 2) **Real-world application:** Applied to a model predicting chromatin accessibility, where the identified clusters correctly mapped to known regulatory motifs.
AI.conclusion: CUTTIE provides a statistically sound way to bridge the gap between 'black-box' genomic deep learning models and biological interpretability.

title: Genetic weight of a mutant in a biparental Moran model with infinite selection
summary: We study, after Coron Le Jan (2024), the genetic contribution of a single strongly advantageous mutant in a biparental Moran model under infinite selection. We prove a functional limit theorem for the entire beneficial mutation spreading period: after normalization by \(\sqrt N\), the contributions carried by the advantaged and disadvantaged subpopulations converge jointly in law to a non-degenerate random multiple of an explicit deterministic profile. Randomness is generated during the initial microscopic growth of the mutant lineage and subsequently propagated through the population along a deterministic macroscopic trajectory. At the heart of this phenomenon is an eigenmode martingale that measures the imbalance between the mean genetic weight of the founding ancestor within the two classes; its limiting value provides precisely the random amplitude of the macroscopic profile and is characterized by a smoothing equation.

AI.tldr: The paper establishes a functional limit theorem for the genetic contribution of a single advantageous mutant in a biparental Moran model, showing that the process converges to a deterministic profile with a random amplitude determined by early-stage stochasticity.
AI.motivation: To extend previous research (Coron Le Jan, 2024) by studying the genetic contribution of a single strongly advantageous mutant in a biparental Moran model under infinite selection.
AI.method: Analysis of a biparental Moran model using functional limit theorems and an eigenmode martingale to bridge initial microscopic stochastic growth with deterministic macroscopic trajectories.
AI.result: After normalization by $\sqrt{N}$, the contributions of advantaged and disadvantaged subpopulations converge jointly to a non-degenerate random multiple of a deterministic profile, where the randomness is captured by a smoothing equation.
AI.conclusion: The genetic spread of a beneficial mutation follows a pattern where initial microscopic fluctuations are propagated through the population as a random amplitude applied to a deterministic macroscopic trajectory.

title: Locality-Controlled Out-of-Distribution Guidance for Robust Regulatory DNA Sequence Design
summary: Designing regulatory DNA sequences for targeted gene-expression control is an important challenge. Recent approaches frame this task as property-conditioned generation, where diffusion models trained on natural sequences are guided toward high predicted activity through reward-based fine-tuning or sampling-time guidance. We show that single-reward evaluation can obscure reward-hacking behavior. By decomposing evaluation into property, novelty, and plausibility, we identify an empirically underexplored region of the evaluation space in which all three objectives are satisfied, but no existing baseline succeeds. We postulate that this gap arises because prior methods treat guidance primarily as a matter of magnitude. In regulatory DNA, however, sequence grammar is spatially nonuniform: motif positions are sensitive to perturbation, while background regions allow more exploration. We therefore propose LOCOGEN by reformulating guidance as a problem of locality. LOCOGEN learns an invariant motif mask through sequence-level invariance learning to protect motif positions, while applying OOD damping only to background positions. It operates at sampling time on a frozen diffusion backbone, without retraining the backbone. Across HepG2, K562, and SK-N-SH, LOCOGEN reaches this previously underexplored region of the property-novelty-plausibility space. Code is available at this https URL.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces LOCOGEN, a sampling-time guidance method for DNA diffusion models that prevents reward-hacking by applying localized guidance to protect essential motifs while allowing exploration in background regions.
AI.motivation: Existing property-conditioned generation methods for regulatory DNA often suffer from reward-hacking, where models maximize predicted activity at the expense of sequence novelty and biological plausibility due to a failure to respect spatially nonuniform sequence grammar.
AI.method: The authors propose LOCOGEN, which reformulates guidance as a locality problem. It uses sequence-level invariance learning to create an invariant motif mask, protecting sensitive motif positions while applying out-of-distribution (OOD) damping only to background regions during sampling-time guidance.
AI.result: LOCOGEN successfully navigates the previously underexplored trade-off space where high property activity, high novelty, and high plausibility are simultaneously achieved across HepG2, K562, and SK-N-SH cell lines.
AI.conclusion: By treating DNA guidance as a local rather than global magnitude problem, models can generate high-activity regulatory sequences that maintain biological integrity and structural novelty without requiring backbone retraining.

title: A two-stage diffusion-driven morphogenesis model with evolving connectivity
comment: Submitted to Applied Mathematical Modelling. Animation available at this https URL
summary: Morphogenesis of diatom silica shells involves a sequence of topological transitions: initially separate ribs grow and branch, then merge through bridges, leaving a regular network of pores. Existing models based on diffusion-limited aggregation or reaction-diffusion reproduce either branching or pore formation, but not both within a single framework. Here we propose a two-stage model of diffusion-driven morphogenesis with evolving connectivity. The model is formulated on a fixed finite element mesh with a density field on an active layer. Stage 1 reproduces dendritic growth, where a stimulus based on the local diffusive flux exceeds a threshold. Stage 2 uses an inverted stimulus, where high local flux suppresses precipitation, stabilizing pores between the dendrites. The update rules are analogous to sensitivity in density-based topology optimization and to strain energy density in bone remodeling. The model predicts distinct morphological regimes on each stage, controlled by the respective thresholds. For a reference calculation, the predicted pore network is regular, with approximately uniform spacing, and pores are absent near the domain edges, consistent with observations on diatom valves. The model provides a unified framework for describing both stages of silica morphogenesis and suggests a route for comparing computational predictions with cryo-electron tomography data.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes a unified two-stage mathematical model to explain the complete morphogenesis of diatom silica shells, bridging the gap between dendritic branching and pore formation.
AI.motivation: Existing models (diffusion-limited aggregation or reaction-diffusion) are fragmented; they can simulate either the branching ribs or the pore networks, but cannot simulate both within a single continuous process.
AI.method: A two-stage diffusion-driven model implemented on a finite element mesh using a density field approach.
AI.result:
The model successfully transitions through two phases: 
1. **Stage 1 (Dendritic Growth):** High diffusive flux triggers precipitation (analogous to bone remodeling).
2. **Stage 2 (Pore Stabilization):** An inverted stimulus where high flux suppresses precipitation, creating regular pore networks.
AI.conclusion: The model produces regular, uniform pore structures that match biological observations (diatom valves) and offers a framework for validating computational models against cryo-electron tomography data.

title: Nonequilibrium Transient Centers in Continuous-Time Systems
summary: Analysis of mathematical models in ecology and epidemiology often emphasizes asymptotic dynamics, such as stable equilibria, periodic orbits, and attractors. However, many biologically relevant trajectories exhibit long transient dynamics in which a relevant observable evolves slowly for an extended period before a comparatively rapid transition occurs. On finite time scales relevant to data collection, management, and intervention, such transient behavior can be more informative than the eventual asymptotic outcome. In this work, we study long-lasting and slowly varying transient dynamics in continuous-time systems through the framework of nonequilibrium transient centers. These centers are points in the state space near which the observable can remain nearly constant for a long time, even when the full state is not near an equilibrium. We develop finite-time escape criteria for identifying such centers and their reachable counterparts. These criteria provide practical conditions under which nearby trajectories can remain in a slow regime for a long period of time before eventually leaving it. We apply the theory to an epidemic model with delay of stability loss. In this model, trajectories may remain close to the disease-free manifold for a long time before the infectious population resurges. The framework developed here describes this behavior as slow evolution near a nonequilibrium transient center followed by finite-time escape from the slow regime.

AI.tldr: Introduces a framework to study long-lasting, slowly varying transient dynamics in continuous-time systems using nonequilibrium transient centers and finite-time escape criteria.
AI.motivation: Standard mathematical models focus on asymptotic dynamics, but biologically relevant phenomena often involve long-lasting transient behaviors that are more informative on finite time scales than eventual equilibrium states.
AI.method: Development of a framework for nonequilibrium transient centers and reachable counterparts, including the derivation of finite-time escape criteria to identify slow-varying regimes in continuous-time systems.
AI.result: The ability to identify points in state space where observables remain nearly constant for extended periods, successfully applied to an epidemic model to explain delayed resurgence of infectious populations.
AI.conclusion: The proposed framework of nonequilibrium transient centers and finite-time escape criteria effectively describes systems where trajectories exhibit slow evolution near a non-equilibrium state before a rapid transition, as demonstrated in epidemic models.

title: Microswimmers lose by swimming selfishly
summary: At low Reynolds number, microswimmers are coupled by the flows they create, even when they are apart. The best way for each swimmer to push itself forward then depends on its neighbors, turning swimming together into a game. To study this, we optimize the shape changes of soft swimmers, alone and in pairs, with a differentiable Stokes solver. From random initial membrane motions, a lone swimmer converges to a traveling membrane wave. In a pair, the stroke of a swimmer affects its neighbor far more than the neighbor affects its own best stroke. For swimmers in line, this influence decays as $1/\ell$ with their separation $\ell$, whereas the incentive to respond decays as $1/\ell^2$. Selfish swimmers, which maximize their own payoff, respond only to the weak incentive. The cooperative gain they miss decays only as $1/\ell^2$, and their selfish adaptations leave the pair worse off than if both had kept their solitary strokes. Related swimmers, which also value the payoff of their neighbor, recover this gain, whereas competitors pay to hinder each other, both following a law that we derive analytically. Hydrodynamics alone thus makes swimming in company a social dilemma, whose outcome depends on how much the swimmers value each other.

AI.tldr: Because the benefit of cooperating decays faster than the physical influence of neighbors, microswimmers naturally fall into 'selfish' traps unless they are evolutionarily incentivized to value their neighbors.
AI.motivation: To understand how much the flow created by one microswimmer influences the propulsion efficiency of its neighbors.
AI.method: The researchers used a differentiable Stokes solver to optimize the membrane shape changes of soft swimmers, comparing solitary movement against group dynamics (pairs/lines).
AI.result:
1. **Influence vs. Incentive:** A swimmer's stroke affects neighbors significantly ($1/	ext{distance}$), but the motivation to change one's own stroke to help neighbors is much weaker ($1/	ext{distance}^2$).
2. **Social Outcomes:**
   - **Selfish Swimmers:** Fail to cooperate, leading to lower efficiency than if they had remained solitary.
   - **Related Swimmers (Altruistic):** Recover efficiency gains through mutual value.
   - **Competitors:** Actively hinder one another, following analytically derived laws of interference.
AI.conclusion: Hydrodynamic coupling at low Reynolds numbers transforms microswimmer coordination into a social dilemma.

title: A richness-sensitive Acoustic Biodiversity Index from species-level detections: classifier benchmarking, false-positive control and validation against standard soundscape indices in an African savanna and an urban zoo
comment: 35 pages, 16 figures, 7 tables; supplementary tables and figures included
summary: Acoustic indices are widely used as rapid proxies for biodiversity, but they summarise the distribution of sound energy rather than the species producing it and often track richness poorly. We revise and test an Acoustic Biodiversity Index (ABI) built from species-level detections. Its primary form, ABI_E, is Shannon diversity of detections normalised by the regional species pool expected at the site and season (H / ln S_ref); temporal stability T is reported as a separate component. We first benchmarked four classifiers on a strongly labelled tropical dataset (1,216 calls, 24 classes) with recording-grouped cross-validation. BirdNET embeddings + logistic regression performed best (macro-F1 0.750 +/- 0.029), and random frame-level splits inflated accuracy from 0.41 to 0.70. We then applied BirdNET v2.4 with a location and season filter to recordings from a riverine savanna in the Zambezi Valley, Zimbabwe, and from three habitats at Emirates Park Zoo and Resort, Abu Dhabi, United Arab Emirates. A stricter post-hoc location filter removed 517 high-confidence detections of 9 implausible species, all at the zoo. After diel-matched rarefaction to equal effort (6 h), the savanna site held 21 species (Hill number 1D = 9.83; ABI_E = 0.38) against 1.3-13 species (ABI_E = 0.03-0.21) at the zoo sites. Across 149 recorded hours, ABI_E correlated strongly with richness (Spearman rho = 0.93), whereas six standard indices did not (best: ACI, rho = 0.48). The stability term was lower at the savanna site (0.39) than at the zoo (0.65-0.67), showing that it penalises the natural diel cycle of bird activity. Species-level indices with explicit false-positive control, a declared regional reference pool and effort standardisation provide a more interpretable biodiversity indicator than energy-based acoustic indices.

AI.tldr: The authors propose a new Acoustic Biodiversity Index (ABI_E) based on species-level detections, which outperforms standard energy-based indices by correlating strongly with actual species richness.
AI.motivation: Traditional acoustic indices summarize sound energy distribution rather than species presence, often failing to track biodiversity richness effectively.
AI.method: The study introduces ABI_E (Shannon diversity of species-level detections normalized by the regional species pool) and evaluates it against standard energy-based indices using classifiers (BirdNET, logistic regression) and rarefaction for effort standardization across tropical and zoo habitats.
AI.result: ABI_E showed a strong correlation with species richness (Spearman rho = 0.93), significantly outperforming standard indices like ACI (rho = 0.48) and providing a more accurate proxy for biodiversity.
AI.conclusion: Species-level indices with explicit false-positive control, a regional reference pool, and effort standardization provide a more interpretable and accurate biodiversity indicator than traditional energy-based acoustic indices.

title: Physiological Trajectories and Observation Patterns in ICU Mortality Prediction: Transportability Under Changing Measurement Conditions
comment: 10 pages, 3 figures, 3 tables. Supplementary material available as an ancillary file
summary: Objective: To distinguish the transferable predictive value of physiological trajectories from that of observation patterns in ICU mortality prediction, and to assess whether measurement timing affects performance independently of observation quantity. Materials and Methods: In-hospital mortality was predicted at 48 hours using MIMIC-III, MIMIC-IV, and eICU. Nested representations progressively integrated latest-value snapshots (R1), longitudinal physiological summaries (R2), and measurement frequency and timing features (R3). Models fitted on 7,762 MetaVision patients were evaluated on 21,682 MIMIC-IV patients and 43,878 eICU patients across 204 hospitals. The effect of measurement timing was assessed while holding the number of retained observations constant. Results: Physiological trajectories improved external prediction in eICU (R2-R1 log-loss difference -0.00922, 95% CI -0.01148 to -0.00704). Observation-pattern features improved locally developed eICU models (R3-R2 -0.00257, 95% CI -0.00370 to -0.00146), but not clearly after transfer from MetaVision (-0.00012, 95% CI -0.00206 to +0.00208). R3 was favoured in 10 of 30 source bootstrap refits. At matched observation counts, retaining measurements spread throughout the window reduced log loss relative to random retention by 0.03280 for R3 versus 0.00703 for R2. Removing the final 12 hours increased log loss relative to count-matched random removal by 0.01947 for R3 versus 0.00822 for R2. Under reduced availability, the local R3 increment changed from beneficial to harmful. Discussion: Physiological trajectories transferred more consistently, while observation-pattern features were particularly sensitive to the timing and availability of measurements. Conclusion: Clinical prediction models should be evaluated not only in new patient populations but also under the measurement conditions that supply their inputs.

AI.tldr: The study found that while physiological trajectories are more robust for external transfer, observation patterns are highly dependent on measurement timing and availability, necessitating evaluation under varied clinical conditions.
AI.motivation: To distinguish the transferable predictive value of physiological trajectories versus observation patterns and to assess how measurement timing affects performance independently of observation quantity.
AI.method: Comparison of nested representations (R1: snapshots, R2: longitudinal summaries, R3: frequency/timing) used to predict 48-hour mortality across MIMIC-III, MIMIC-IV, and eICU datasets.
AI.result: Physiological trajectories (R2) showed more consistent external transferability; observation patterns (R3) improved local models but failed to transfer well and were highly sensitive to measurement timing and availability.
AI.conclusion: Clinical prediction models should be evaluated not only on new patient populations but also under varying measurement conditions (timing and availability) to ensure reliability.
